issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a single-patient assault trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because it implies multiple victims or identification with other victims rather than the patient's own assault experience. A more self-referential trigger would be expected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
issues.explanation: 'Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening' sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile's self-directed shame and identity-change appraisals. It implies confidence that another person would have prevented the assault, which conflicts with the patient's own vulnerability/self-blame framing in a way that is hard to integrate clinically.

issues.item: Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma in a 70-year-old male, 'medical procedures' plus 'body shame' implies a strong bodily injury/medical aftermath theme, but the rest of the profile does not support that theme. With only offender cues and intrusive thoughts otherwise present, the medical trigger looks insufficiently anchored and may be mismatched to the rest of the assault profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body shame' is not impossible after assault, but alongside 'defective self' and 'unrecognisable self' it suggests a bodily violation/injury-focused appraisal pattern that is not well reflected in the other selected nodes. The triggers and strategies mainly reflect avoidance, numbing, and offender-related activation rather than body-focused trauma processing.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising others' is weakly connected to the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation links Triggers strongly with Maladaptive Strategies and Negative Appraisals strongly with Triggers, but this strategy is not a plausible direct response to the chosen triggers (medical procedures, intrusive thoughts, offender cues) and is not well explained by the selected appraisals. It addresses a generalized harm concern that is otherwise absent from the profile.

vignette:
Gerald is a 70-year-old married man who has spent the better part of four decades working as a salesperson, a career built on warmth, easy conversation, and the kind of confident sociability that once came naturally to him. He presented for an initial assessment several weeks after what he described, with visible reluctance, as "something that happened to me that I should have been able to stop." The event he was referring to was a physical assault that occurred approximately eight months ago in the parking lot of a bar he had visited after a late sales call. A man - someone Gerald recognized as a difficult acquaintance from his professional circle - approached him while heavily intoxicated, and what began as a heated argument escalated quickly into a sustained physical attack. Gerald was struck repeatedly, left on the ground, and did not seek medical attention that night, telling himself it was nothing serious. He has not told his wife the full account.

In the weeks following the assault, Gerald began noticing that certain things pulled him back to the parking lot with a force that felt involuntary. The smell of alcohol - encountered at client dinners, at the bar cart his company keeps at quarterly meetings - would arrive before he could prepare himself, and suddenly he was not in a conference room but on cold asphalt. Unwanted thoughts intruded throughout the day, often without any obvious prompt, surfacing mid-conversation or in the silence before sleep. Most acutely, the possibility of seeing the man who attacked him - a prospect that is not remote, given their overlapping professional world - produced a vigilance so consuming that Gerald began scanning rooms before entering them. These intrusions, each time they arrived, triggered an urgent need to manage what felt unmanageable: he began avoiding the street where the bar was located, rerouting his sales calls to stay clear of that part of the city, and throwing himself into deliberate thought suppression, mentally redirecting whenever the memory surfaced. He also described a growing habit of emotional flattening - "I just turn it off," he said - a numbness he had come to rely on as a kind of internal insulation against the worst of what the intrusions carried.

What the intrusions also carried, and what Gerald found harder to name, were the appraisals they deposited each time they surfaced. When an unwanted thought broke through, or when the smell of alcohol stopped him cold at a client dinner, he did not only feel frightened - he felt implicated. He had come to believe, with a quiet but durable conviction, that the assault had happened because of the way he had spoken that night, the tone he had used, the fact that he had not walked away sooner. There was something wrong with him, he was certain - a fundamental defectiveness that the event had simply revealed. The person who now rerouted his drives, who numbed himself at family gatherings, who could not finish a glass of wine without his chest tightening, was unrecognisable to him. That sense of estrangement from himself had become one of the most distressing features of his presentation. And crucially, the appraisals did not stay still - they fed back into the intrusions themselves, so that the thought of seeing his attacker carried not only fear but a kind of anticipated confirmation: that he would freeze again, that his defectiveness would be visible, that the encounter would prove what he already suspected about himself. The loop was self-sustaining in a way Gerald could not articulate but clearly felt.

His occupational life had quietly contracted. Client meetings in unfamiliar venues required advance reconnaissance. He had declined two evening events in the past month, offering vague excuses to colleagues who had begun to notice his withdrawal. His wife knew something had changed but not what, and the distance between what she observed and what he permitted her to know had become its own source of strain.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was a moment at a quarterly sales meeting when the smell of a colleague's whiskey reached him across the table and he excused himself and did not return. He sat in his car for forty minutes. He told the intake clinician that he was not afraid of being assaulted again. What he was afraid of, he said quietly, was that this was simply who he was now.
